headline_draft: Auros study: 43% of US consumers feel duped by AI ads; 44% avoid brands using AI in marketing
summary: <anite index="65-3,65-4">Auros commissioned Talker Research to survey 4,000 adults in the U.S., U.K. and Australia from August 26 to September 1, 2026. In the U.S. sample, 43% said they had felt duped by a product advertised with AI, 53% said they do not trust AI-advertised products to be described accurately, and 44% said they go out of their way to buy from brands that do not use AI in their ads.</anite> <anite index="65-5,65-6">Only 20% of U.S. respondents correctly identified real products that had been enhanced with AI. Shoppers in the Auros study cannot reliably spot AI in an ad, and they penalize the brand when they believe they have.</anite> <anite index="64-5,64-6">The majority of respondents say they plan to use AI for some part of their holiday shopping this year (55% of U.K. adults, 54% of U.S. adults, and 48% of Australians), with common planned uses including finding the best prices, comparing product reviews, finding gift ideas and discovering deals.</anite>
why_pm: This reveals a critical consumer-trust asymmetry: shoppers embrace AI as a *tool* (helping them decide) but resist it as a *persuader* (brands using it to influence them). For PMs building commerce products, agent-based recommendations, or AI-powered marketing workflows, this data signals that transparency and user agency matter more than AI sophistication. Trust erodes when consumers feel AI is used *on them* rather than *for them*.
key_facts: 43% US consumers felt duped by AI-advertised products
53% don't trust AI-advertised products to match descriptions
44% actively avoid brands using AI in ads
Only 20% can correctly identify AI-enhanced products
Consumers question AI vs. real products 4 times per week on average
54% US, 55% UK plan to use AI for holiday shopping
72% see AI as helpful for finding prices and comparing reviews
61% believe at least one brand type uses misleading AI marketing
quotes: There's a fascinating trust divide emerging around AI in commerce. Consumers are skeptical when AI is being used to persuade them, but much more receptive when they're the ones using AI to make a better decision.

headline_draft: Model PM job pays 60% premium over traditional PM roles; only ~75 specialists exist globally
summary: <anite index="6-2,6-10">Model PM has become the most lucrative sub-field inside of product management, with a 60% premium over PMs outside AI. The gap is similar at the mid, senior, and staff levels.</anite> <anite index="6-13,6-14">Madhu Guru led product for Gemini and Veo, plus Nano Banana, and he's now a senior director of AI at Meta. He estimated fewer than 75 people globally have the depth needed for this role.</anite> <anite index="6-15">Barkley works at Luma AI, which, valued at $4B, has one of the best video models.</anite>
why_pm: This quantifies an emerging scarcity: the skills to manage frontier AI models, LLM-based products, or agentic systems command a 60% salary premium, yet only ~75 people globally have credible depth. If John wants to level up into AI product leadership or is considering a career move, this signals the premium talent commands—and explains why companies are acquiring specialized teams (Rocket/Geniez) rather than hiring individual contributors.
key_facts: Model PM median base pay is highest across all PM specializations
60% salary premium over non-AI PMs at all career levels (mid, senior, staff)
Estimated <75 specialists globally with credible model PM depth
Top practitioners often move to director or exec roles (e.g., Madhu Guru at Meta)
Typical career path: foundation model expertise → product lead at AI company → director/exec at big tech
Examples: Luma AI ($4B valuation) leads with experienced model PMs
